name: Clinical Decision Support
title: Clinical Decision Support
answer: Clinical decision support covers software that helps a clinician reason about a patient at the point of care, from drug interaction and dosing checks to sepsis alerts, diagnostic suggestions and risk scores. It sits inside the wider field of clinical documentation and ambient intelligence, where the same encounter produces both a note and a set of prompts. The scope runs from simple rule based reminders embedded in an electronic health record to models that read the chart and propose a differential. It is distinct from documentation tools that only transcribe, because the output is meant to change a clinical choice rather than record one.

sections.body: Clinical decision support covers software that helps a clinician reason about a patient at the point of care, from drug interaction and dosing checks to sepsis alerts, diagnostic suggestions and risk scores. It sits inside the wider field of clinical documentation and ambient intelligence, where the same encounter produces both a note and a set of prompts. The scope runs from simple rule based reminders embedded in an electronic health record to models that read the chart and propose a differential. It is distinct from documentation tools that only transcribe, because the output is meant to change a clinical choice rather than record one.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most deployed systems run inside the electronic health record or alongside it through a standards based interface, drawing on structured data such as labs, vitals, medications and problem lists, and increasingly on unstructured notes. Ambient systems add a capture layer, a microphone or room device, plus speech recognition and a summarisation model, so the same pipeline that drafts a note can also surface a suggestion. Compute is usually split between vendor cloud services and on premises inference where patient data cannot leave the network.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Rule based logic still carries most high stakes alerts, because a threshold or an interaction table can be inspected and explained. Model based support is built by training on retrospective cohorts, then validating on held out data and often on a second site before any live use. Evaluation looks at sensitivity, specificity, alert burden and whether clinicians actually act on the output, since an ignored alert has no effect. Deployment is usually staged, with silent running first, then a limited pilot, then wider release with monitoring for drift and for changes in clinician behaviour.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: In the United States, some decision support falls under device regulation and some does not, and the boundary depends on the claims made and the level of clinician independence.Provenance matters in both directions, meaning which data trained the model and which evidence supported a given alert at a given moment. Records of model version, input data and the clinician's response are the practical backbone of any audit or defence. This page describes practice and is not legal or medical advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward fewer, better alerts and more context aware support that arrives inside the documentation workflow rather than as a separate interruption. Ambient capture is pushing decision support closer to the conversation, which raises the question of when a suggestion should appear and when it should stay silent. Expect more attention to alert fatigue, to local validation before go live, and to logging that can reconstruct why a prompt fired. The open question is not whether models can produce a plausible suggestion, but whether the surrounding workflow, evidence trail and accountability can carry it.
